title: Auditing Emergent LLM-Agent Collaboration through Cooperation-Obligation Coupling
summary: LLM-agent systems can solve complex tasks through dynamic self-organization and emergent cooperation. Auditing this process is essential because plausible intermediate or final outputs can conceal incomplete or unsupported work and poorly allocated responsibility, ultimately compromising response quality. While existing approaches may record messages, tool calls, provenance, or task dependencies, an auditability gap exists as they do not jointly represent what work remains, who is responsible for it, and what evidence justifies each work-state transition. We address this auditability gap by proposing \emph{Integrated Cooperation-Obligation REpresentation} (iCORE). It creates a unified encoding $X=(G,Q,Π)$ integrating observable interactions as a cooperation graph $G$, evolving work and assignments as an obligation graph $Q$, and the audit map $Π$ linking them with verifiable properties and evidence. This iCORE representation enables the auditor to certify two complementary properties: {Work soundness}, where every active decision-relevant work assertion must have a finite justification through $G$ and $Π$; and {Agent-assignment stability}, which requires that no feasible alternative agent improve the declared contribution value for an evaluated obligation by more than $ε$. We establish local-to-global soundness and assignment-regret guarantees and a performance bound under stated conditions. iCORE is an instrumentation layer over workflows. Numerical results show that the full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes and that, relative to passive full-state observation, iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of $11.5\%$ and $26.4\%$ in controlled and real-LLM execution, respectively, with corresponding absolute terminal-performance improvements of $15.1\%$ and $31.0\%$.

AI.tldr: iCORE is an instrumentation layer that provides a unified representation framework X=(G,Q,Π) for auditing LLM-agent systems by integrating cooperation graphs (observable interactions), obligation graphs (work and assignments), and audit maps (verifiable properties and evidence) to certify work soundness and agent-assignment stability, achieving 11.5-31.0% trajectory and terminal performance improvements.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent systems solve complex tasks through dynamic self-organization, but auditing is challenging because plausible outputs can conceal incomplete work, poor responsibility allocation, and compromised quality. Existing approaches (message recording, tool calls, provenance, task dependencies) fail to jointly represent what work remains, who is responsible, and what evidence justifies work-state transitions, creating an auditability gap.
AI.method:
The paper proposes Integrated Cooperation-Obligation Representation (iCORE) with unified encoding X=(G,Q,Π):
- Cooperation graph G: encodes observable interactions
- Obligation graph Q: represents evolving work and assignments
- Audit map Π: links G and Q with verifiable properties and evidence

Certifies two properties: (1) Work soundness - every active decision-relevant work assertion has finite justification; (2) Agent-assignment stability - no feasible alternative agent improves contribution value by more than ε. Establishes local-to-global soundness, assignment-regret guarantees, and performance bounds.
AI.result: iCORE is implemented as an instrumentation layer over workflows. Numerical results show: (1) Full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes; (2) iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of 11.5% (controlled) and 26.4% (real-LLM) compared to passive full-state observation; (3) Corresponding terminal-performance improvements of 15.1% and 31.0% respectively.
AI.conclusion: iCORE addresses the auditability gap by providing a unified representation that enables certifying work soundness and agent-assignment stability in LLM-agent systems. The approach demonstrates significant performance improvements in both controlled and real LLM executions, establishing it as a practical instrumentation layer for ensuring response quality and responsibility allocation in autonomous agent systems.

title: Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness
summary: AI agents are moving into production workflows where they retrieve information, call tools, maintain state, and act on behalf of users or organizations, but many release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not show whether an agent is ready to operate under production constraints. Capability is therefore not production readiness. This paper introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents. PAI combines four dimensions of deployment evidence: Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance. Evaluation measures observed behavior, Context measures the operating environment that shapes that behavior, Compliance measures alignment with applicable rules and controls, and Governance measures whether the organization can authorize, monitor, audit, and control the agent during operation. PAI is implemented inside ProofAgent Harness, an open source infrastructure for auditable AI agent evaluation and governance. Validation across two heavily regulated domains, healthcare and finance, shows that PAI carries held out readiness signal and separates higher risk from lower risk configurations. The results show that context engineering strongly changes reliability, capability improves behavior but does not determine readiness, and governance evidence must remain visible rather than averaged away. PAI reframes agent release from a faith based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision.

AI.tldr: PAI is a governance readiness index combining Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance dimensions to transform agent release from faith-based to auditable decisions.
AI.motivation: AI agents are entering production workflows, but release decisions rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not demonstrate production readiness under real constraints.
AI.method: PAI integrates four dimensions: Evaluation (observed behavior), Context (operating environment), Compliance (alignment with rules/controls), and Governance (authorization, monitoring, audit, control). Implemented in open-source ProofAgent Harness.
AI.result: Validation in healthcare and finance shows PAI separates high-risk from low-risk configurations; context engineering strongly changes reliability; capability improves behavior but does not determine readiness; governance evidence must remain visible, not averaged away.
AI.conclusion: PAI reframes agent release from a faith-based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision, providing a rigorous governance framework for production AI agents.

title: Scaling LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Systems: Design Principles and Architectural Scalability Analysis
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems have the potential to enable collective intelligence and scale toward solving highly complex tasks through coordinated ensembles of specialized agents. However, despite their theoretical potential, the architectural design space remains largely non-systematized and lacks broadly established design principles. Furthermore, the scalability characteristics of such systems are only partially understood so far. This paper makes two contributions. We first distill four design principles for scalable MAS architectures from a structured analysis of prior work: simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, and summary-based communication. We operationalize these principles in a reference architecture whose topology is formalized as a constrained directed workflow graph, and we evaluate four configurations of increasing complexity on a standardized benchmark of terminal-based system engineering tasks using two LLMs of differing capability. Our findings show that scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the underlying LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity, then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. In addition, persistent consistency issues emerge as a central challenge across all scaling levels. These results provide concrete design guidance for practitioners and highlight consistency and evaluation standardization as key targets for future research.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes and formalizes design principles for scalable LLM-based multi-agent systems, showing that scaling yields accuracy improvements with linear cost growth only when the LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold, though performance degrades at high complexity due to consistency issues.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems have theoretical potential for collective intelligence and complex tasks, but the architectural design space lacks systematic principles and scalability characteristics are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors distill four design principles (simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, summary-based communication) into a reference architecture formalized as a constrained directed workflow graph, then evaluate four configurations on a terminal-based system engineering benchmark using two LLMs.
AI.result: Scaling produces measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity, then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. Persistent consistency issues emerge across all scaling levels.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide concrete design guidance for practitioners and highlight consistency and evaluation standardization as key targets for future research.

title: Argonaut: Interactive Visual Exploration for Distributed Optimization
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures. Accepted in ACSOS 2026 [artifacts track]
summary: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings is often hard to explore and navigate: disentangling what other agents choose, how their choices are interdependent, and how they collectively reach a global objective quickly becomes intractable as the system scales. The major limitation is observability of the search process. Existing methods are largely centralized and offer limited support, visualizing only the final solution or providing algorithm backends over a fixed dataset, so how a solution is reached stays a black box. We present Argonaut, a lightweight, containerized optimization dashboard that enables interactive, visual exploration of the entire search process for multi-agent discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings. Users upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify the decision space and its parameters on the fly, and run multiple algorithm backends to inspect how each configuration shapes local agent decisions and the resulting global objective. By uniting system construction, optimization, and analysis in one interactive loop, the first of its kind, Argonaut makes distributed discrete-choice optimization a human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot, black-box computation. We evaluate Argonaut on real-world household-electricity, shared-mobility, and sensor-data-exchange datasets scaling to 5600 agents and up to 1M solutions under brute force. Built on a Node.js interface with extensible Java and Python optimization backends, it maintains a typical runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.

AI.tldr: Argonaut is an interactive, containerized dashboard for visualizing and exploring the entire search process of distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings, allowing users to modify decision spaces in real-time and inspect how configurations affect both local agent decisions and global objectives.
AI.motivation: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings is difficult to explore due to limited observability of the search process. Existing methods are centralized and primarily visualize only final solutions or algorithm backends over fixed datasets, leaving the solution process as a black box.
AI.method: Argonaut is a lightweight, containerized optimization dashboard built on Node.js with extensible Java and Python optimization backends. It enables users to upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify decision spaces and parameters on the fly, run multiple algorithm backends, and inspect how each configuration shapes local decisions and global objectives in an interactive loop.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world datasets (household-electricity, shared-mobility, sensor-data-exchange) scaling to 5600 agents and up to 1M solutions. Argonaut maintains typical runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Argonaut unites system construction, optimization, and analysis in one interactive loop, making distributed discrete-choice optimization a human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot, black-box computation.

title: Compact Representation of Mipmapped SVBRDFs via Shared Gaussians
summary: Spatially-varying BRDFs (SVBRDFs) are central to material representation in computer graphics, but their high-resolution, multi-channel, mipmapped textures impose a substantial storage burden. Existing compression methods face a fundamental trade-off: block-based compression provides random access and hardware-friendly decoding but exploits redundancy only within local blocks; image codecs offer strong rate-distortion performance but are not designed for direct real-time texture access; and neural texture compression achieves high compression ratios but requires neural inference during decoding, which introduces additional runtime overhead, especially on mobile platforms. We present Gaussian Texture Compression (GTC), a compact 2D Gaussian-based representation for mipmapped SVBRDF texture stacks that delivers high-quality compression with flexible rate-distortion trade-offs. Our method is based on a key observation that there are two dominant sources of redundancy in such data: across mip levels and across material maps. Both share a common underlying structure: the same spatial support is reused, with only level- or map-specific information attached. This property naturally suits 2D Gaussians, since each Gaussian explicitly separates its spatial footprint from the values it carries, allowing the footprint to be shared while the values vary per level and per map. Building on this property, GTC shares Gaussians along both redundancy dimensions and is trained via a progressive optimization pipeline. Experiments show that GTC achieves higher reconstruction quality and lower memory usage than ASTC, the industry-standard GPU texture compression format, while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding suitable for real-time rendering.

AI.tldr: Gaussian Texture Compression (GTC) is a compact 2D Gaussian-based representation for mipmapped SVBRDF texture stacks that delivers high-quality compression with flexible rate-distortion trade-offs, outperforming ASTC while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding for real-time rendering.
AI.motivation: SVBRDFs require high-resolution, multi-channel, mipmapped textures that impose substantial storage burden. Existing compression methods face fundamental trade-offs: block-based compression exploits only local redundancy; image codecs offer strong rate-distortion but lack real-time texture access; neural texture compression achieves high ratios but requires inference overhead, especially on mobile platforms.
AI.method: GTC leverages the observation that SVBRDF data has two redundancy sources (across mip levels and material maps) sharing common spatial support structure. The method uses 2D Gaussians that separate spatial footprints from carried values, enabling Gaussians to be shared along both dimensions while values vary per level and map. Trained via progressive optimization pipeline with random-access, non-neural decoding.
AI.result: GTC achieves higher reconstruction quality and lower memory usage than ASTC (industry-standard GPU texture compression format) while supporting random-access, non-neural decoding suitable for real-time rendering.
AI.conclusion: GTC provides an effective balance between compression quality, memory efficiency, and computational efficiency for SVBRDF textures, addressing the storage burden of high-resolution, multi-channel, mipmapped SVBRDFs without the runtime overhead of neural inference methods.

title: It's Not Just More Demos: Counterfactual Action Sensitivity Coverage for Data-Efficient Robust Robot Imitation
comment: Workshop paper accepted at the RSS 2026 Workshop on Data-Centric Robotics: What Data Do Robots Really Need?
summary: Visuomotor imitation learning has demonstrated success for manipulation tasks. However, the trained policies remain brittle to visual `nuisances', with even minor task-preserving variations such as lighting, distractions or changes in colour result in heavy degradation of the trained policy's performance. While increasing data diversity can improve robustness, it is unclear which additional demonstrations are informative for a particular trained policy. We propose Counterfactual Nuisance Behaviour Cloning (CFNBC), an offline data-selection framework for targeted robustness repair. Starting from a nominal policy trained on `clean' demonstrations, CFNBC generates paired clean and nuisance observations that preserve the expert action, then measures \emph{action drift}: the change in the policy's predicted action under a nuisance that should not alter the desired behaviour. This provides a policy-specific sensitivity signal for selecting a compact, response-diverse repair set from a larger candidate pool, without requiring rollout success labels or online policy execution. We show in MuJoCo bimanual cube transfer and SimplerEnv cube stacking that action drift correlates with nuisance-induced failure, and that response-guided repair with only $20$--$30$ selected candidates substantially outperforms matched-budget random selection while approaching the performance of much larger random repair budgets. These results support a data-centric view of robustness repair: the most useful data are not necessarily the most numerous, visually diverse, or obviously difficult, but the examples that cover fragile response modes of the current policy.

AI.tldr: CFNBC is an offline data-selection framework that uses action drift as a sensitivity signal to select a compact repair set for improving visuomotor imitation learning robustness to visual nuisances.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor imitation learning policies are brittle to visual nuisances (lighting, distractions, color changes), even though increasing data diversity can improve robustness. It's unclear which additional demonstrations are informative for a particular trained policy.
AI.method: Starting from a nominal policy trained on clean demonstrations, CFNBC generates paired clean and nuisance observations preserving expert actions and measures action drift (change in predicted action under nuisance). This sensitivity signal selects a compact repair set from a candidate pool without rollout labels or online execution.
AI.result: Action drift correlates with nuisance-induced failure. Response-guided repair with only 20-30 selected candidates substantially outperforms matched-budget random selection and approaches performance of much larger random repair budgets, demonstrating on MuJoCo bimanual cube transfer and SimplerEnv cube stacking.
AI.conclusion: Supports a data-centric view of robustness repair: the most useful data are not necessarily the most numerous, visually diverse, or obviously difficult, but examples that cover fragile response modes of the current policy.

title: $Σ$-Mem: An Online Reliability Memory for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Memory is central to long-horizon LLM agents, yet existing memory systems primarily preserve interaction content rather than modeling which agents can be trusted and under what conditions. This limitation is particularly important in multi-agent systems, where a central model may be unable to directly verify plausible or correlated peer responses. We introduce $Σ$-Mem, an online reliability memory that records historical competence evidence for individual peers and peer relationship evidence across the peer set. Both forms of evidence are maintained as real symmetric states and updated from post-decision correctness feedback. By Weyl's inequality, the spectral change caused by each event-level update is bounded, enabling stable online adaptation without retraining the underlying models. $Σ$-Mem provides a general write-and-read interface: the same memory can be used for residual steering of a central model, response-free peer routing, or reliability-weighted voting. Across five Qwen-family models, $Σ$-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts and generalizes to unseen peers and task domains. Direct memory readouts also outperform majority voting and the best fixed peer over the full OOD evaluation set. Moreover, performance improves consistently as more correctness feedback becomes available, indicating that $Σ$-Mem progressively accumulates actionable reliability information. These results establish reliability memory as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: Σ-Mem is an online reliability memory for LLM agents that maintains competence evidence for individual peers and relationship evidence across peer sets, using Weyl's inequality for stable online adaptation without retraining. It provides a general write-and-read interface for residual steering, peer routing, and reliability-weighted voting, outperforming baseline methods across multiple Qwen models.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems preserve interaction content but fail to model which agents can be trusted and under what conditions, particularly problematic in multi-agent systems where central models cannot directly verify peer responses. This limitation is critical for long-horizon LLM agents requiring adaptive coordination.
AI.method: Σ-Mem maintains two types of real symmetric state evidence: historical competence evidence for individual peers and peer relationship evidence across the peer set. Both are updated from post-decision correctness feedback. Using Weyl's inequality, the spectral change caused by each event-level update is bounded, enabling stable online adaptation without retraining underlying models. The system provides a general write-and-read interface for residual steering of a central model, response-free peer routing, or reliability-weighted voting.
AI.result: Across five Qwen-family models, Σ-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts and generalizes to unseen peers and task domains. Direct memory readouts outperform majority voting and the best fixed peer over the full OOD evaluation set. Performance consistently improves as more correctness feedback becomes available, indicating progressive accumulation of actionable reliability information.
AI.conclusion: Reliability memory establishes a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems, demonstrating that tracking trustworthiness evidence rather than just interaction content enables more robust, adaptive agent collaboration.

title: A Query-Efficient Stochastic Volume Rendering Framework for Time-Varying Implicit Neural Volumes
summary: Time-varying implicit neural representations (INRs) provide a compact representation of scientific volumes and, for modalities such as dynamic X-ray computed tomography (CT), are often the only practical way to represent the data. However, interactive volume rendering of INRs is challenging, as cheap memory lookups are replaced by expensive neural inferences, hindering the performance. Therefore, conventional volume rendering methods such as ray marching with dense sampling are often impractical. While resampling, caching, and retraining can mitigate this cost, they compromise convenience and accuracy and become impractical for time-varying data. We tackle these challenges using a query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework based on delta tracking. Our system employs a four-stage pipeline that exploits heterogeneous parallelism, using ray tracing cores for traversal and tensor cores for batched neural evaluation. Furthermore, we present strategies to reduce INR queries via ray budgeting and query pruning, thereby increasing per-frame performance. Using our renderer, many time-varying INRs can be rendered directly from their original representation. The system achieves ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU and converges to high-fidelity images. Moreover, the system enables interactive temporal exploration of the continuous domain, with timestep updates taking approximately 1-2 ms.

AI.tldr: A query-efficient stochastic volume rendering framework using delta tracking and heterogeneous parallelism to enable interactive rendering of time-varying implicit neural representations (INRs).
AI.motivation: Time-varying INRs provide compact representations for scientific volumes (e.g., dynamic CT) but are challenging to render interactively because neural inferences replace cheap memory lookups, making conventional ray marching impractical. Existing solutions like resampling, caching, and retraining compromise convenience and accuracy.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline exploiting heterogeneous parallelism: ray tracing cores for traversal and tensor cores for batched neural evaluation. The system uses delta tracking for stochastic volume rendering and strategies including ray budgeting and query pruning to reduce INR queries.
AI.result: The system achieves ~30-40 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution on an RTX 4090 GPU, converges to high-fidelity images, and enables interactive temporal exploration with timestep updates taking approximately 1-2 ms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework makes time-varying INRs practical for interactive volume rendering and scientific visualization, allowing direct rendering from their original representation without compromising accuracy or convenience.

title: Simulation of Surgical Suturing Using Position-Based Dynamics and the Material Point Method for Robot Reinforcement Learning
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, accepted for the IEEE RAS/EMBS 11th International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (BioRob 2026)
summary: Recent advances in robotics research have created a strong demand for high-performance simulators. Surgical robotics simulation faces unique challenges due to the need to model diverse objects, such as rigid instruments, soft tissue, and fluids. While many studies simulate sutures or soft tissue independently, only a few have considered the complete soft-tissue suturing scenario, including the contact between sutures and deformable tissue during suture insertion. Building on previous work, this paper presents a novel suturing simulation environment using sutures modelled by position-based dynamics (PBD) and soft bodies modelled by the material point method (MPM) while considering two-way contact with frictional and drag forces. We introduce a contact coupling method between the PBD suture and the MPM soft tissue, enabling visually plausible suture-tissue interactions. The simulator is optimized for GPU execution with parallel scenes using multiple CUDA streams, and we present a Reinforcement Learning (RL) environment for autonomous suturing sub-tasks, including needle insertion, driving, and extraction. Using ML-Agents, RL agents trained in the simulator show stable learning and achieve 80% and 68% success rates in needle insertion and extraction, respectively, under the strictest distance threshold.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel GPU-optimized surgical suturing simulation environment using position-based dynamics (PBD) for sutures and material point method (MPM) for soft tissue, with a contact coupling method enabling realistic suture-tissue interactions. The simulator integrates a Reinforcement Learning framework for autonomous suturing tasks, achieving 80% and 68% success rates in needle insertion and extraction, respectively.
AI.motivation: Surgical robotics simulation faces unique challenges due to the need to model diverse objects: rigid instruments, soft tissue, and fluids. Most existing studies simulate sutures or soft tissue independently, but few have considered the complete soft-tissue suturing scenario, including the contact between sutures and deformable tissue during suture insertion.
AI.method:
The paper introduces a novel suturing simulation environment with the following components:
1. Sutures modeled using position-based dynamics (PBD)
2. Soft bodies modeled using the material point method (MPM)
3. Two-way contact with frictional and drag forces
4. A contact coupling method between PBD sutures and MPM soft tissue for visually plausible suture-tissue interactions
5. GPU optimization using parallel scenes with multiple CUDA streams
6. A Reinforcement Learning (RL) environment for autonomous suturing sub-tasks (needle insertion, driving, extraction) using ML-Agents
AI.result: RL agents trained in the simulator demonstrate stable learning. They achieve 80% success rate in needle insertion and 68% success rate in needle extraction under the strictest distance threshold, validating the effectiveness of the proposed simulation environment for training surgical robotics algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully integrates PBD and MPM with contact coupling to create a visually plausible surgical suturing simulation. The GPU-optimized implementation enables efficient training of RL agents, demonstrating practical applicability for developing autonomous surgical robotic systems. The success rates achieved validate the simulator's fidelity for training and evaluating surgical manipulation algorithms.

title: VISA: A Structured Description Protocol for Agent-Based Simulation Models Towards Machine Reproducibility
summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) are difficult to reproduce: their behavior is spread across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, so that two readers routinely reconstruct different models from the same documentation. We present VISA, a structured, symbol-based description protocol that specifies a model in eight interconnected tables---four at the agent level (Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function) and four at the model level (Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation)---under the principle of minimality with completeness. VISA makes a model machine-parseable and unambiguous via two artifacts: nineteen executable consistency rules that turn model validity into a checkable property, and three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, and code generation) that operationalize the full author--check--code--reproduce loop. We validate the protocol on three external, independently authored ABMs spanning three platforms: we reproduce two cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from their VISA specifications, and we capture a third, an industrial AnyLogic model, in eight tables (passing all nineteen rules) while honestly demarcating where reproduction is blocked by a proprietary movement library and unavailable data---itself a transparency contribution. VISA moves the reproduction barrier from the model, where it is invisible, to a named, localized dependency, where it is actionable.

AI.tldr: VISA is a structured, symbol-based description protocol for agent-based models (ABMs) that specifies models in eight interconnected tables, nineteen executable consistency rules, and three LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, code generation), enabling machine-parseable and unambiguous ABM specifications that improve reproducibility by moving barriers from invisible model assumptions to named, localized dependencies.
AI.motivation: ABMs are difficult to reproduce because their behavior is spread across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, causing different readers to reconstruct different models from the same documentation.
AI.method: VISA specifies ABMs in eight interconnected tables (four at agent level: Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function; four at model level: Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation) following the principle of minimality with completeness. The protocol includes nineteen executable consistency rules that transform model validity into a checkable property and three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, code generation) to operationalize the full author-check-code-reproduce loop.
AI.result: Validation on three external, independently authored ABMs spanning three platforms: (1) reproduced two cross-language ABMs (NetLogo to Python) directly from VISA specifications; (2) captured an industrial AnyLogic model in eight tables, passing all nineteen rules; (3) identified blocked reproduction due to a proprietary movement library and unavailable data, demonstrating the protocol's transparency contribution.
AI.conclusion: VISA moves the reproduction barrier from the model (where it is invisible) to a named, localized dependency (where it is actionable), enhancing ABM transparency and reproducibility by making model specifications machine-parseable, unambiguous, and systematically checkable.

title: Corrigible Assistance in One Round: Pragmatic-Pedagogic Best Response
comment: World Symposium on the Algorithmic Foundations of Robotics (WAFR) 2026
summary: Assistance games formalize human-robot collaboration under asymmetric information: the human knows the goal, while the robot must infer it from observation and interaction in order to assist effectively. In general, computing optimal assistance game strategies online is intractable, since exact solutions require planning in a POMDP. We identify a class of assistance games in which pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning resolves goal uncertainty in a single time step, rendering the full-horizon game exactly solvable by a tractable best-response procedure. Within this class, we show that mainstream inverse optimal control exhibits an inference ceiling that hinders alignment, while pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning overcomes this barrier by immediately disambiguating goals through actions that look equivalent under task execution alone. Finally, we validate our theoretical results and proposed method on a simple collaborative block-building example.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes assistance games for human-robot collaboration where the human knows the goal and the robot must infer it through observation and interaction. The authors identify a class of games solvable by pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning that resolves goal uncertainty in one time step, overcoming the inference ceiling of mainstream inverse optimal control.
AI.motivation: Human-robot collaboration under asymmetric information is challenging because robots must infer human goals from observations, which typically requires solving POMDPs that are computationally intractable. Existing inverse optimal control methods have an inference ceiling that limits alignment with human intentions.
AI.method: The authors define a class of assistance games where pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning resolves goal uncertainty in a single time step, making the full-horizon game exactly solvable via a tractable best-response procedure. They compare this approach against mainstream inverse optimal control, demonstrating how pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning immediately disambiguates goals through actions that appear equivalent under task execution alone.
AI.result: They show that pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning overcomes the inference ceiling of inverse optimal control, enabling immediate goal disambiguation. The method is validated on a collaborative block-building task, demonstrating successful human-robot collaboration under asymmetric information.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a tractable framework for human-robot collaboration in assistance games by leveraging pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning. The approach resolves goal uncertainty in a single step, overcoming limitations of existing inverse optimal control methods and enabling more effective human-robot alignment.

title: AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Understanding large codebases is a long-horizon task for Large Language Model (LLM) agents: answering a single question can require building and running the software, tracing execution across files, and synthesizing evidence over tens of minutes. On SWE-Atlas QnA, a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) resolves only 32.3% of tasks. Dividing the work among agents with clean contexts mitigates this limitation. However, the subtasks of code comprehension are interdependent. One agent's findings can rewrite another's task, so agents must coordinate during execution, not only at phase boundaries. Existing multi-agent systems support such exchange only between phases, through staged handoffs or synchronized rounds. Communication and work remain mutually exclusive. A discovery made mid-execution cannot be shared until the next boundary. We present AgentRadio, an asynchronous message-passing layer that equips coding-agent harnesses with three primitives: threads, messages, and waiting for mentions. The last runs as a background task, surfacing teammates' messages without interrupting foreground work, so each agent remains passively aware of its peers and folds new findings into its ongoing task. Under a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, four agents organized by AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of tasks, 29.8 points above a single agent and above Claude Code with the newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%). Rubric-level analysis shows the gain growing with task difficulty, consistent with mid-course correction as the underlying mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Coral-Protocol/AgentRadio.

AI.tldr: AgentRadio is an asynchronous message-passing system that enables LLM coding agents to coordinate mid-execution, improving task resolution from 32.3% (single agent) to 62.1% (four agents) on the SWE-Atlas QnA benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle with long-horizon codebase understanding; existing multi-agent systems only support coordination between phases, making communication and work mutually exclusive. A single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) only resolves 32.3% of tasks on the SWE-Atlas QnA benchmark.
AI.method: AgentRadio introduces an asynchronous message-passing layer with three primitives: threads, messages, and a background "waiting for mentions" task. It implements a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, allowing agents to passively receive updates without interrupting foreground work.
AI.result: Four agents using AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of tasks, a 29.8-point improvement over a single agent and exceeding Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (57.2%). Performance gains grow with task difficulty, consistent with improved mid-course correction.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous message-passing enables real-time coordination during execution, allowing agents to integrate new findings into ongoing work. This approach transforms multi-agent systems from phase-boundary handoffs to continuous collaboration, significantly enhancing long-horizon code comprehension capabilities.

title: Failure Detection for Surgical Robot Imitation Policies via Flow-Matching World Modeling
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Imitation learning has shown increasing promise for autonomous robotic surgery, yet safe deployment remains challenging due to the safety-critical nature of surgical tasks and the complexity and variability of surgical environments. Failure detection is therefore an essential safeguard, but its development remains difficult due to the challenges of scarce failure data, highly variable manipulation dynamics, and the need to balance missed detections against disruptive false alarms. To address these challenges, we introduce FoMo-FD (Flow-Matching World Model for Failure Detection), a failure detection method that learns nominal short-horizon visual dynamics with an action-conditioned flow-matching world model. FoMo-FD scores the inverse-transport nonconformity of observed endpoint latents, enabling window-level detection of visual-action inconsistencies without requiring failure demonstrations. Detection thresholds are obtained by conformal calibration on successful executions, yielding task-specific alarms without assuming future failure types. We evaluate FoMo-FD on four surgically relevant manipulation tasks with twenty failure modes across simulation and real-world experiments using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). Results show that FoMo-FD outperforms observation-level anomaly baselines and a prediction-error variant of the same world model, with the wrist-camera view achieving the strongest performance, including a 96.6% failure detection rate (FDR) at a 1.3% false alarm rate (FAR).

AI.tldr: FoMo-FD is a failure detection method for robotic surgery that uses a flow-matching world model to score visual-action inconsistencies via inverse-transport nonconformity, achieving 96.6% failure detection rate at 1.3% false alarm rate on surgically relevant tasks using the da Vinci Research Kit.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning for autonomous robotic surgery requires reliable failure detection due to safety-critical tasks, scarce failure data, variable manipulation dynamics, and the need to balance missed detections against disruptive false alarms.
AI.method: FoMo-FD learns nominal short-horizon visual dynamics using an action-conditioned flow-matching world model. It scores inverse-transport nonconformity of observed endpoint latents for window-level detection without requiring failure demonstrations. Detection thresholds are obtained via conformal calibration on successful executions.
AI.result: FoMo-FD outperforms observation-level anomaly baselines and a prediction-error variant. On four manipulation tasks with twenty failure modes, the wrist-camera view achieved 96.6% failure detection rate (FDR) at 1.3% false alarm rate (FAR) across simulation and real-world experiments using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK).
AI.conclusion: FoMo-FD effectively addresses the challenges of failure detection in surgical robotics by enabling task-specific alarms through conformal calibration on successful executions, eliminating the need for failure demonstrations, and achieving strong performance on both simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

title: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
summary: Social learning is a powerful mechanism through which agents learn about the world from others. However, humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning, which can carry time and cognitive resource costs. How do people balance social and non-social learning? We propose a Rational Mentalizing model of the decision to engage in social learning. This model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and the informativeness of their future actions. It then weighs the utility of social learning against the utility of non-social learning. Using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment, we show that the Rational Mentalizing model can quantitatively capture human trade-offs between these strategies. These findings suggest that selective social learning is guided by 'Theory of Mind' in the service of utility maximization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Rational Mentalizing model to explain how humans balance social learning (observing others) with non-social learning (direct exploration), showing that selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind reasoning about others' goals and the informativeness of their actions.
AI.motivation: Humans often have the choice between social learning (observing others) and non-social learning (direct exploration), but the balance between these strategies is not fully understood. The authors aim to develop a model that explains this trade-off by incorporating mentalizing (Theory of Mind) capabilities into rational decision-making.
AI.method: The researchers developed a Rational Mentalizing model that estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goals and the informativeness of their future actions, then weighs this against the utility of non-social learning. They tested this model using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment themselves.
AI.result: The Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between social and non-social learning strategies in the experimental game. The findings demonstrate that people's choices between these strategies follow the predictions of the model.
AI.conclusion: Selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind reasoning in the service of utility maximization. Humans use mentalizing capabilities to assess whether observing others will provide useful information, leading to more efficient learning than pure random exploration.

title: Cross-Embodiment Transfer via Behavior-Aligned Representations
summary: Recent progress in large-scale imitation learning for robot manipulation has been driven by leveraging datasets across a wide range of robot embodiments. However, achieving significant cross-embodiment transfer is often still challenging. In this work, we study the role of using behavior-aligned representations (e.g., object bounding boxes, language motions, end-effector traces of robot motion) in vision-language-action (VLA) models to promote cross-embodiment transfer. We hypothesize that by possessing invariances across embodiments while being predictive of robot actions, these representations can help unify large-scale cross-embodiment data to enhance transfer. To assess our hypothesis, we develop a simulation-based benchmark designed to assess transfer with diverse cross-embodiment data to new embodiments. Using this benchmark, we compare different representations and ways of incorporating them. We identify that end-effector traces can be particularly beneficial for transfer, representations are generally more useful with larger prior datasets, and can be used to benefit from action-free data. We also demonstrate that they can enhance sim-to-real cross-embodiment transfer, improving task completion progress of real robot policies pre-trained on simulation data by 28%. We provide videos of our evaluations at our website: https://ajaysridhar.com/barx/.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates behavior-aligned representations (bounding boxes, language motions, end-effector traces) in vision-language-action models to improve cross-embodiment transfer in robot manipulation. Using a simulation benchmark, the authors demonstrate that end-effector traces significantly enhance transfer, especially with large prior datasets, and improve sim-to-real task completion by 28%.
AI.motivation: Cross-embodiment transfer remains challenging despite progress in large-scale imitation learning for robot manipulation. The authors seek to understand how behavior-aligned representations can unify cross-embodiment data to enhance transfer capabilities.
AI.method: A simulation-based benchmark was developed to assess transfer with diverse cross-embodiment data. The authors compared different representations (object bounding boxes, language motions, end-effector traces) and their incorporation methods across various scenarios including action-free data scenarios.
AI.result: End-effector traces were found to be particularly beneficial for transfer. Representations were more useful with larger prior datasets and could leverage action-free data. The approach enhanced sim-to-real cross-embodiment transfer, improving real robot task completion progress by 28%.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-aligned representations, particularly end-effector traces, significantly improve cross-embodiment transfer in robot manipulation. These representations can unify cross-embodiment data, benefit from large prior datasets, and enhance sim-to-real transfer performance.

title: A Systems Engineering Framework for Vision-Language-Enabled UAV Triage and Disaster Response
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures. Author accepted manuscript of AIAA Paper 2026-4010, published in the AIAA AVIATION 2026 Forum
summary: Recent advances in Vision Language Models (VLMs) have created new opportunities for disaster response, where responders must interpret large volumes of sensor data under time pressure. Current VLM applications include social media monitoring for situational awareness, generation of draft action plans, and translation of technical alerts into public-facing messages. While these efforts can accelerate information flow, they remain largely limited to decision-support roles. Such approaches can increase operator burden because humans must still translate outputs into coordinated actions across teams and robotic assets. This study explores the viability of embedding VLMs as coordination agents within the human-UAV loop. The proposed architecture integrates natural language interaction, mission-level task coordination, software-in-the-loop implementation, and communication aligned with the Incident Command System (ICS). Rather than functioning solely as advisory tools, VLMs facilitate communication between human operators, mission control logic, and UAV task execution. The framework was developed using a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach, with use case and block definition diagrams representing system roles, internal structure, and component interactions. Three key elements, the VLM Coordinator Agent, UAV Mission Control, and Task Allocator, were implemented within an integrated simulation and control environment. A preliminary human-factors evaluation with seven participants showed reduced perceived workload across mental demand, effort, and frustration, along with high ratings for AI trust and communication clarity. By integrating MBSE, software-in-the-loop testing, and human-factors evaluation, this work advances scalable human-autonomy teaming for high-stakes disaster response, with broader implications for aerospace autonomy and civil safety.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating Vision Language Models (VLMs) as coordination agents within the human-UAV loop for disaster response, using Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and software-in-the-loop testing to reduce operator workload and enhance human-autonomy teaming.
AI.motivation: Recent VLM advances have created opportunities for disaster response, but current applications are limited to decision-support roles where humans must still translate outputs into coordinated actions, increasing operator burden. The study aims to explore embedding VLMs as active coordination agents rather than advisory tools.
AI.method: The architecture integrates natural language interaction, mission-level task coordination, software-in-the-loop implementation, and Incident Command System (ICS)-aligned communication. Developed using MBSE with use case and block definition diagrams. Three key elements were implemented: VLM Coordinator Agent, UAV Mission Control, and Task Allocator within an integrated simulation environment. A preliminary human-factors evaluation was conducted with seven participants.
AI.result: Preliminary human-factors evaluation demonstrated reduced perceived workload across mental demand, effort, and frustration, along with high ratings for AI trust and communication clarity.
AI.conclusion: By integrating MBSE, software-in-the-loop testing, and human-factors evaluation, this work advances scalable human-autonomy teaming for high-stakes disaster response, with broader implications for aerospace autonomy and civil safety.

title: Arm2Air: Cross-Embodiment Skeleton Transfer for 3D Relay Formation
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) relay networks can restore connectivity after communication infrastructure is damaged. Urban relay placement is difficult because line-of-sight blockage, communication range, altitude, and three-dimensional obstacles must be considered jointly. Arm2Air transfers obstacle-avoidance skeletons from robot arms to UAV relay placement through cross-embodiment transfer. Source-domain robot-arm motions from a pretrained Neural MP model are converted into ordered skeletons that pretrain a transformer-based transfer platform, which is then adapted to the UAV domain using limited target data and Low-Rank Adaptation. The transferred skeleton initializes a relay chain that is refined for connectivity, bottleneck capacity, delay, and movement cost. On nine held-out high-clutter 3D urban maps, Arm2Air reduced median end-to-end planning runtime by 64.9 percent relative to the fastest conventional planner. On the high-obstruction group of a separate 30-map dense urban holdout, it increased bottleneck capacity by 32.6 percent, reduced capacity variance by 74.7 percent, reduced maximum hop distance by 13.2 percent, reduced hop-distance variance by 75.2 percent, and reduced relay displacement by 16.9 percent relative to IMPC-MD. With only three target-domain training maps, Arm2Air reduced relay-position root mean square error by 53.6 percent relative to training from scratch while updating 0.134 million parameters, compared with 1.383 million for Scratch and Full Fine-tuning. These results demonstrate computationally and data-efficient UAV relay placement and suggest a broader principle for transferring ordered structural priors across heterogeneous embodied tasks.

AI.tldr: Arm2Air transfers obstacle-avoidance skeletons from robot arms to UAV relay placement using cross-embodiment transfer with a transformer-based platform and Low-Rank Adaptation, enabling computationally and data-efficient relay placement in cluttered urban environments.
AI.motivation: UAV relay networks can restore connectivity after communication infrastructure damage, but urban relay placement is challenging due to the need to jointly consider line-of-sight blockage, communication range, altitude, and three-dimensional obstacles.
AI.method: Arm2Air converts source-domain robot-arm motions from a pretrained Neural MP model into ordered skeletons to pretrain a transformer-based transfer platform. The platform is adapted to the UAV domain using limited target data and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The transferred skeleton initializes a relay chain that is refined for connectivity, bottleneck capacity, delay, and movement cost.
AI.result: On nine held-out high-clutter 3D urban maps, Arm2Air reduced median end-to-end planning runtime by 64.9% relative to the fastest conventional planner. On a 30-map dense urban holdout, it increased bottleneck capacity by 32.6%, reduced capacity variance by 74.7%, reduced maximum hop distance by 13.2%, reduced hop-distance variance by 75.2%, and reduced relay displacement by 16.9% relative to IMPC-MD. With only three target-domain training maps, Arm2Air reduced relay-position RMSE by 53.6% while updating 0.134M parameters, compared to 1.383M for training from scratch.
AI.conclusion: Arm2Air demonstrates computationally and data-efficient UAV relay placement and suggests a broader principle for transferring ordered structural priors across heterogeneous embodied tasks.

title: LabEvolver: Training-Free Experience Evolution for Safe and Grounded Wet-Lab Agents
summary: We introduce LabEvolver, a training-free framework that equips safe and grounded wet-lab agents with episodic memory from execution experience. LabEvolver couples a state-grounded inner trial loop for adaptive perception, online planning, and safety validation with an outer evolution loop that distills completed trajectories into reusable skill, strategy, and safety experience. On robotic solution-preparation tasks, LabEvolver demonstrates real-world feasibility, reducing pH-regulation completion time and safety-gate intercepts by 48.2% and 60.0%, respectively. On ALFWorld, it further improves cumulative success rate within 20 steps from 76.2% with ReAct to 91.4% over 500 continual tasks, showing generality beyond wet-lab settings. These results support learn-by-doing experience evolution as a feasible path toward closed-loop automated scientific discovery. The project page is available at https://github.com/AndyGao6186/LabEvolver.

AI.tldr: LabEvolver is a training-free framework that equips safe and grounded wet-lab agents with episodic memory from execution experience, combining a state-grounded inner trial loop with an outer evolution loop to distill completed trajectories into reusable skills, strategies, and safety experience.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for wet-lab agents to learn from execution experience, enabling learn-by-doing evolution as a feasible path toward closed-loop automated scientific discovery.
AI.method: LabEvolver consists of two coupled loops: (1) an inner trial loop with state-grounded adaptive perception, online planning, and safety validation; and (2) an outer evolution loop that distills completed trajectories into reusable skill, strategy, and safety experience. The framework is training-free.
AI.result: On robotic solution-preparation tasks, LabEvolver reduced pH-regulation completion time by 48.2% and safety-gate intercepts by 60.0%. On ALFWorld, it improved cumulative success rate from 76.2% (with ReAct) to 91.4% over 500 continual tasks, demonstrating generality beyond wet-lab settings.
AI.conclusion: The results support learn-by-doing experience evolution as a viable approach toward closed-loop automated scientific discovery.

title: Write-Safe Flow Field Mapping under Ambiguous Onboard Sensing and Localization Drift
summary: Mobile robots can infer local flow structure from onboard sensing, but a locally plausible estimate is not always safe to write into a global map. Similar flow structures may produce ambiguous observations, while localization drift causes predicted patches to be written at incorrect locations. Repeated misregistered updates then accumulate into persistent ghost structures. We address this failure mode with a map-reference-aware conservative fusion framework. The model predicts a local velocity patch and a learned write-safety score that continuously attenuates uncertain map updates while permitting initialization when no reliable map reference is available. Across synthetic jet and crossflow environments, the proposed method reduces average ghost contamination by 42% relative to ungated fusion. A zero-shot hardware replay using real pressure and optical-flow measurements from a thruster wake further reduces ghost contamination by 39% while retaining 81% map coverage. These results show that safe map writing is critical for flow mapping under ambiguous sensing and localization drift.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a map-reference-aware conservative fusion framework for mobile robots to safely write local flow structure estimates into global maps. The method uses learned write-safety scores to attenuate uncertain updates while permitting initialization when no reliable map reference is available.
AI.motivation: Mobile robots face a critical challenge: locally plausible flow structure estimates can lead to persistent "ghost structures" in global maps when similar flow patterns cause ambiguous observations or when localization drift misregisters predicted patches. These errors accumulate through repeated misregistered updates, creating false features that degrade mapping accuracy.
AI.method: The proposed framework implements a conservative fusion approach with two key components: (1) a local velocity patch prediction model, and (2) a learned write-safety score that continuously attenuates uncertain map updates. The system permits map initialization only when no reliable map reference is available, providing a safety mechanism for ambiguous situations.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements: the method reduces average ghost contamination by 42% compared to ungated fusion approaches. A zero-shot hardware replay using real pressure and optical-flow measurements from thruster wakes further reduces ghost contamination by 39% while maintaining 81% map coverage, demonstrating robust performance across both synthetic and real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: Safe map writing is essential for reliable flow mapping under conditions of ambiguous sensing and localization drift. The proposed conservative fusion framework effectively mitigates ghost structure formation, enabling more trustworthy global map construction in challenging flow environments.

title: RedFlow: Redirect Failure into Action-Level Corrections for Flow-matching VLA Policy
summary: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have shown strong potential for robotic manipulation but often suffer from compounding errors caused by distribution shifts during deployment. While offline reinforcement learning (RL) provides a practical way to improve deployed policies using rollout data, existing methods either ignore failure data or exploit it only at the trajectory level, resulting in low learning efficiency and persistent errors. We propose **RedFlow**, a fine-grained offline RL framework that redirects failure experiences into action-level corrective supervision for flow-matching VLA policies. RedFlow consists of two key components: (1) a **Context-Aware Corrective Matching** mechanism that identifies failure-inducing actions and retrieves successful alternatives from similar contexts as corrective targets, and (2) an **Adaptive Redirection Objective** that jointly reinforces successful actions, suppresses undesirable ones, and redirects recoverable failures toward corrective targets. By converting both successful and failed experiences into dense supervision, RedFlow enables robust recovery learning from mixed-quality data. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark and three real-world manipulation tasks show that RedFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline RL baselines, improving the real-world success rate from 56.7% to 74.7%. It also matches strong on-policy methods (PPO, GRPO, and DDPO) while requiring roughly an order of magnitude fewer training samples.

AI.tldr: RedFlow is a fine-grained offline RL framework that redirects failure experiences into action-level corrective supervision for flow-matching VLA policies, improving real-world success rates from 56.7% to 74.7% while matching strong on-policy methods with an order of magnitude fewer training samples.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching VLA policies suffer from compounding errors due to distribution shifts. Existing offline RL methods either ignore failure data or exploit it only at trajectory level, resulting in low learning efficiency and persistent errors.
AI.method: RedFlow consists of (1) Context-Aware Corrective Matching that identifies failure-inducing actions and retrieves successful alternatives from similar contexts as corrective targets, and (2) an Adaptive Redirection Objective that jointly reinforces successful actions, suppresses undesirable ones, and redirects recoverable failures toward corrective targets.
AI.result: On LIBERO benchmark and three real-world manipulation tasks, RedFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline RL baselines, improving real-world success rate from 56.7% to 74.7%, while matching strong on-policy methods (PPO, GRPO, DDPO) with roughly an order of magnitude fewer training samples.
AI.conclusion: RedFlow enables robust recovery learning from mixed-quality data by converting both successful and failed experiences into dense supervision, achieving significant performance improvements over existing methods.

title: DexDirect: Direct Kinesthetic Arm Guidance for Efficient Dexterous Demonstration Collection
summary: Scalable collection of dexterous manipulation demonstrations remains a major bottleneck for robot learning. High-fidelity interfaces often require costly hardware and extensive setup, while low-setup, low cost alternatives tend to provide less precise control and impose greater cognitive workload on operators. We present DexDirect, a direct kinesthetic arm guidance for efficient dexterous demonstration collection. The operator drags a 6-DoF gravity-compensated robot arm directly by a handle, while a single webcam retargets operator's other hand onto a 16 joints 13-DoF dexterous robot hand. User studies suggest DexDirect collects 17.2x and 3.2x more successful demonstrations compared to purely vision (AnyTeleop) and pose-tracking (TeleDex) baselines. An adapted NASA-TLX shows DexDirect greatly reduces mental demand, effort, and frustration, despite raising physical demand. A diffusion policy trained on DexDirect demonstrations reaches a 90% success rate on a cube pick-and-place task. These results suggest that direct kinesthetic arm guidance combined with vision-based hand retargeting provides an efficient low-setup and scalable interface for collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations

AI.tldr: DexDirect enables efficient dexterous demonstration collection through direct kinesthetic arm guidance (6-DoF gravity-compensated robot arm) combined with single-webcam hand retargeting to a 13-DoF dexterous hand, achieving 17.2x and 3.2x more successful demonstrations than vision and pose-tracking baselines respectively, with 90% pick-and-place success using diffusion policies.
AI.motivation: Scalable collection of dexterous manipulation demonstrations is a bottleneck. High-fidelity interfaces require costly hardware and extensive setup, while low-setup, low-cost alternatives provide less precise control and impose greater cognitive workload on operators.
AI.method: DexDirect combines direct kinesthetic arm guidance with vision-based hand retargeting: operators drag a 6-DoF gravity-compensated robot arm via a handle, while a single webcam retargets the operator's other hand onto a 16-joint 13-DoF dexterous robot hand for demonstration collection.
AI.result: User studies show DexDirect collects 17.2x and 3.2x more successful demonstrations compared to AnyTeleop (vision) and TeleDex (pose-tracking) baselines. NASA-TLX shows reduced mental demand, effort, and frustration despite increased physical demand. A diffusion policy trained on DexDirect demonstrations achieves 90% success rate on cube pick-and-place.
AI.conclusion: Direct kinesthetic arm guidance combined with vision-based hand retargeting provides an efficient, low-setup, and scalable interface for collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

title: RoboBRIDGE: A Modular Framework for Bridging Policies to Robust Real-World Robotic Agents
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have attracted growing interest as a scalable approach to robotic manipulation. While these models are effective action predictors, deploying them as robotic agents exposes critical gaps: no mechanism for failure recovery, inconsistent execution over long horizons, and limited robustness to shifts in observations, tasks, or embodiments. Existing solutions address these limitations individually through model retraining or environment-specific modules, yet what is needed is a general framework that systematically transforms a pretrained VLA into a robotic agent. We present RoboBRIDGE, a modular framework that provides an orchestration layer over five coordinated modules, namely Monitor, Perceptor, Planner, Controller, and Robot Interface, to compose robust robotic agents from off-the-shelf components, including pretrained VLAs. The Monitor pairs rapid failure detection with hierarchical recovery to correct errors before they cascade. When the environment diverges from the current plan, the Planner triggers replanning while the Perceptor updates scene understanding asynchronously, avoiding execution stalls. Within the Controller, primitive skill fine-tuning factors manipulation into domain-invariant primitives with dedicated LoRA adapters, reducing sensitivity to domain shifts when a VLA is used. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world case studies spanning multiple robot platforms and VLA backbones, RoboBRIDGE consistently outperforms both standalone policies and prior augmented VLA deployments. These results suggest that reliable robotic agency does not arise from scaling action predictors alone, but from structured orchestration around them.

AI.tldr: RoboBRIDGE is a modular orchestration framework that transforms pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models into robust robotic agents by coordinating five specialized modules: Monitor (failure detection), Perceptor (scene understanding), Planner (replanning), Controller (skill fine-tuning with LoRA), and Robot Interface.
AI.motivation: VLA models excel as action predictors but lack critical capabilities for deployment: no failure recovery mechanism, inconsistent long-horizon execution, and limited robustness to observation/task/embodiment shifts. Existing solutions address these individually through retraining or environment-specific modules, but a general framework is needed.
AI.method: RoboBRIDGE provides an orchestration layer with five coordinated modules: Monitor (rapid failure detection with hierarchical recovery), Perceptor (asynchronous scene understanding updates), Planner (triggers replanning when environment diverges), Controller (uses primitive skill fine-tuning with LoRA adapters for domain-invariant manipulation), and Robot Interface (hardware connection).
AI.result: Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world case studies spanning multiple robot platforms and VLA backbones, RoboBRIDGE consistently outperforms both standalone policies and prior augmented VLA deployments.
AI.conclusion: Reliable robotic agency emerges not from scaling action predictors alone, but from structured orchestration around them. The framework demonstrates that modular coordination of existing components can achieve robustness that single-model approaches cannot.

title: Static In, Dynamic Out: Counterfactual Action Augmentation for Moving Object Manipulation
summary: Visuomotor policies have advanced on manipulation tasks where the target object stays static during execution, but real deployments break this assumption: parts drift on conveyors and fruits sway in the wind. We introduce Static In, Dynamic Out (SIDO), a counterfactual action augmentation that enables a policy trained only on static object demonstrations to adapt to unseen object motion at test time. Our key idea is to factorize moving object manipulation into two sub-problems: predicting where the object will be, and reaching that predicted pose. SIDO displaces the object to a counterfactual future position and morphs the demonstrated action chunk to preserve the hand-object relative pose, yielding a goal-conditioned policy. At deployment an object pose predictor supplies the future position. Across three simulated tasks (Mug, Square, Stack) under five object motion patterns and two real-world tasks (Gantry, Peachtree), SIDO improves moving object success over the baselines while preserving static object performance. Project website: https://sido-staticindynamicout.github.io/.

AI.tldr: SIDO (Static In, Dynamic Out) introduces counterfactual action augmentation to enable policies trained on static object demonstrations to adapt to unseen moving objects at test time.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies have excelled at manipulation tasks with static objects but fail when objects move (e.g., on conveyors or in the wind). Real-world deployments often require handling dynamic objects, creating a gap between simulated training and real-world performance.
AI.method: SIDO factorizes moving object manipulation into two sub-problems: predicting object future positions and reaching those poses. It displaces the object to counterfactual positions and morphs demonstrated action chunks to preserve hand-object relative pose, yielding a goal-conditioned policy. At test time, an object pose predictor provides future positions.
AI.result: Evaluated on 3 simulated tasks (Mug, Square, Stack) with 5 motion patterns and 2 real-world tasks (Gantry, Peachtree). SIDO improves moving object success over baselines while maintaining static object performance.
AI.conclusion: SIDO successfully enables policies trained solely on static demonstrations to generalize to unseen object motions, effectively bridging the gap between static and dynamic manipulation scenarios.

title: Learning Social Robot Navigation By Sensing Human Legs
summary: Robots navigating among pedestrians typically sense their surroundings with a 2D LiDAR mounted close to the ground. At that height, the sensor mostly sees moving legs rather than whole people, yet most learning-based navigation methods still treat pedestrians as simple shapes like circles. This paper addresses that gap with CALF (Convolutional Attention for Leg Features), an end-to-end neural architecture that combines convolutional layers, attention, and MLP to interpret leg motion directly from LiDAR scans and produce safe navigation commands. The CALF policy is trained using deep reinforcement learning algorithms within LegNav, a custom lightweight 2D simulator that combines 2D LiDAR ray tracing with a novel pedestrian gait model. The resulting policy is compared against classical and learning-based baselines in terms of navigation performance and social compliance. The approach is validated through real-world experiments via zero-shot deployment on a TurtleBot 4, yielding smooth and socially compliant trajectories. Written in JAX, the LegNav simulator enables the training of a deployment-ready CALF policy in under an hour on a single consumer GPU.

AI.tldr: CALF is an end-to-end neural architecture combining convolutional layers, attention, and MLP to interpret leg motion from 2D LiDAR scans and produce safe navigation commands, trained via deep reinforcement learning in the custom LegNav simulator and validated through zero-shot deployment on a TurtleBot 4.
AI.motivation: Most robots navigating among pedestrians use 2D LiDAR mounted low to the ground, which primarily captures moving legs rather than whole people, yet existing learning-based navigation methods typically treat pedestrians as simple shapes like circles. This disconnect between sensor perception and representation limits effective social navigation.
AI.method: CALF (Convolutional Attention for Leg Features) is an end-to-end neural architecture integrating convolutional layers, attention mechanisms, and MLP to interpret leg motion directly from LiDAR scans and generate safe navigation commands. The policy is trained using deep reinforcement learning in LegNav—a custom lightweight 2D simulator written in JAX that combines 2D LiDAR ray tracing with a novel pedestrian gait model. Training completes in under an hour on a single consumer GPU.
AI.result: The CALF policy outperforms classical and learning-based baselines in navigation performance and social compliance. Real-world validation through zero-shot deployment on a TurtleBot 4 demonstrates smooth, socially compliant trajectories without further fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully bridges the gap between low-height LiDAR perception (leg features) and effective pedestrian navigation by using leg motion interpretation directly from sensor data, enabling socially compliant behavior in real-world environments.

title: RaDiVe: Robust 4D Radar Odometry with Distance-Bounded NDT and Velocity-Discrepancy Point Uncertainty
summary: Recent advances in 4D radar enable robust perception in adverse weather; however, the inherent sparsity, noise, and limited positional precision of radar point clouds pose significant challenges for registration-based odometry. In this letter, we propose RaDiVe, a 4D radar odometry framework designed to improve the accuracy and robustness of radar point-cloud registration. We introduce a distance-bounded Normal Distributions Transform (NDT), which improves optimization stability and computational efficiency by restricting the correspondence search to near-distance voxel pairs. To mitigate measurement ambiguity, we propose a velocity-discrepancy point uncertainty model that weights each input 4D radar point according to the discrepancy between its measured Doppler radial velocity and the radial velocity predicted from the estimated ego-velocity. Furthermore, we incorporate Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based surface point extraction via implicit neural mapping to construct a geometrically consistent and noise-filtered local submap. Evaluations across multiple public datasets demonstrate that RaDiVe outperforms existing 4D radar odometry baselines by 44.4% in translational Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and 21.3% in rotational ATE on average, while maintaining real-time performance. The source code will be made publicly available to the robotics community: https://github.com/to-be-open-sourced.

AI.tldr: RaDiVe is a 4D radar odometry framework that improves accuracy and robustness through distance-bounded NDT, velocity-discrepancy point uncertainty model, and SDF-based surface point extraction via implicit neural mapping.
AI.motivation: Recent 4D radar advances enable robust perception in adverse weather, but inherent sparsity, noise, and limited positional precision of radar point clouds pose significant challenges for registration-based odometry.
AI.method: 1. Distance-bounded Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) - restricts correspondence search to near-distance voxel pairs for optimization stability and computational efficiency; 2. Velocity-discrepancy point uncertainty model - weights points based on discrepancy between measured Doppler radial velocity and predicted ego-velocity; 3. Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based surface point extraction via implicit neural mapping for geometrically consistent, noise-filtered local submaps.
AI.result: RaDiVe outperforms existing 4D radar odometry baselines by 44.4% in translational ATE and 21.3% in rotational ATE on average, while maintaining real-time performance.
AI.conclusion: The source code will be made publicly available to the robotics community.

title: UniCross: Unified Cross-Skill Dexterous Manipulation Synthesis
summary: Many dexterous manipulation tasks require the object to remain securely held throughout the interaction. From the perspective of hand-object relational motion, such manipulation comprises four canonical skills: grasping, relocation, in-hand rotation, and in-hand translation. Human hands flexibly compose these skills to accomplish complex tasks. Existing approaches, however, model these skills separately with skill-specific action constraints, objectives, or even dedicated hand morphologies, which breaks the compatibility and continuity required for long-horizon composition. In this work, we present a unified framework that models all four skills in a single formulation that shares the same state and action spaces and a common objective structure.
